The Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago is one of the first central banks to require paper stock to be stamped with a unique serial number and printed with the bank's name. The serial numbers were necessary to identify the paper stocks and to verify the origin of each paper's printing. If one paper was used by different banks in different cities, the serial numbering system would be a challenge to the Federal reserve. Each bank would have to maintain a separate inventory of paper. This was a major cost to banks and the government. Eventually, banks would run out of inventory and would need to purchase paper from the Fed. During the Great Depression, there were about ten central bank paper-printing facilities in the United States. By 1937, thirty-one central paper printing facilities were in operation. Although paper and ink were used to print the central banking systems, paper also made up the largest part of banknotes. In the 1930s, an average of $3.75 billion in banknote was printed each day. Banknote printing was not a highly profitable business, and, in order to keep printing costs down, all paper used for bank notes was recycled or destroyed. For example, if a bank had $2 billion of notes on hand and needed to replace only $1 billion, it could simply print more notes. Some banks chose to destroy their paper notes, while other banks simply recycled their stock of stock certificates.

If you have a long term investment in a stock or fund, and you sell it in the future, the value of the stock will rise or fall depending on how much you bought it for. When you buy the investment, you are actually buying the right to receive the income stream that the company is producing. The company can choose to cut the dividend or increase the price.
For example, if a company produces $1 million in dividends each year, but the dividends are only $500,000 a year (or less), then the market price of that stock is $0.00. However, in this case, it could be argued that you were just buying an option to collect the entire dividend. It is actually a right. If the share price falls below $.01, then you would be stuck with that $100,00 dividend and would have to sell the shares. You would not be able to buy anything else. Your only option would then be to wait until the next year to purchase the same shares at the current price and collect $900,001 in dividend income. Or, your option could still be exercised by selling at $2.50, which would give you a $700,003 dividend (more or less depending upon the number of shares you sold).
You are not only buying a share in an investment company, however. At the time you purchase that share, there is an agreement between the seller and the buyer that says that this particular investment can only be sold in that particular way. This is called a "lockup." The lockup agreement says you cannot sell that investment at a higher price than the original purchase price, or at any price lower than $5, for example. In order to have this share sold at this price or lower, therefore, a buyer must have the agreement from the sellers to do so. Why would the country that is the largest economy in the world want a smaller economy to have a larger currency?
A:
If a small country, such as a banana republic, wants to get into the EU, they would want their currency to be the euro.
This is because the Euro is a "unitary currency" - it is not possible to break up the monetary union of the eurozone into separate pieces, and even if it was, it would be a lot harder to do so than it currently is. 
Since the entire monetary system of Europe is unified, there is no need for the small member countries to control their own money - the central bank in Frankfurt can print whatever it wants, provided it isn't illegal. In the case of a Euro break-up, the member states would have to create new currencies, which would probably be much more difficult than the current situation.

for 2018 An analyst estimate for a company is an estimate of the value of a firm, based on its financial statements. Analysts may use different methods to arrive at the estimate, including the use of multiple estimates, a multiple regression, and other methods. An analyst is a person who makes estimates of corporate value.
The term "analyst" is generally used to refer to an individual analyst of an investment firm. This is distinct from a "fundamental analyst" who is employed by a fund of funds or hedge fund. The latter is considered a specialist in a particular industry or asset class. It is common for many investment analysts to work for more than one investment bank or brokerage firm or to hold multiple investment positions in different investment funds. In addition, many analysts work at hedge funds, mutual funds and private equity firms. There are also investment banks and brokerage firms that provide corporate valuation services to the public. A company that does not offer valuation as a service is known as an "outsourcing firm".
When an analyst makes an estimation, they typically use a variety of inputs. These include the company's financial information (balance sheets, income statements, cash flow statements and cash flows), market information, industry information and competitive information. Other inputs may include valuation techniques and valuation models. Many analysts may have several different sources of information that they use to make an assessment. For example, an independent analyst may look at different valuation sources, such as market valuations, private valuators, competitors, financial analysts and competitors. Another method is to use several valuation methods (e.g., discounted cashflow, discounted income or market capitalization).
A company may be valued in several ways. Generally, the valuation is done by comparing the current valuation to a future valuation. Each valuation method may result in the same valuation, but this does depend on the assumptions used in each method. If the future valuer is based upon current market conditions, then the values may differ. However, if the method used is consistent, it is unlikely to result into a difference in valuation unless there is some fundamental change in market valuation that has not been considered in either valuation process. 
Valuation methods include:
Market Valuation Discounted Cash Flow Equity valuation Price to earnings ratio Capitalization Cost of capital Stock split Debt to equity Net worth Liquidity Total assets Shareholders equity (shareholder equity)

In the case of crude oil, there are two basic types of forecasts: fundamental and technical. Fundamental forecasts are based purely on economic factors, while technical forecasts use the prices for known commodities to predict future price levels. A fundamental forecast of the future of U.S. crude would be a fundamental analysis of economic conditions, or the latest available U6 price index, as a measure of underlying fundamentals. Such forecasts have been used by traders and investors since the early 1970s. Technical forecasts of prices and future supply and demand forecasts can be used to assess the long-term price outlook of commodities. When used in conjunction with fundamental analyses, technical analysis has been found to be an effective way of forecasting future commodity prices. 
As oil prices have risen in recent years, for example, this has led to a decrease in the use of technical forecasting methods and a rise in fundamental forecasts to determine future oil supply. However, some technical forecasters have argued that the forecasting methodology used is fundamentally flawed. They say that forecasts based only on price information can never accurately predict the supply of energy in future periods, and that such forecasts should be rejected altogether. Furthermore, they argue that there is no evidence that they have outperformed fundamental methods in terms of accuracy and reliability. More recently, it has become more popular to use technical models to forecast energy prices, using the same techniques that have led the commodities market to recover from the energy glut of 2008. This has allowed technical analysts to make forecasts that are more accurate than those made by fundamental analysts. Although the forecasts made are of course based in part on technical factors (supply, demand, etc.), they are not predictions based solely on prices but are predictions of price movements based, at least in some cases, on supply factors. The technical forcasts are generally less accurate, however, than the fundamental forcings. Some technical analyses of recent oil forfests have shown that technical prices are sometimes more volatile than fundamental prices as well. As I've mentioned in other posts, I'm a big fan of teaching children how to save money. And I want to share some of the games I teach them to make it more fun.
There are lots of great games out there, some free and some paid, but I like these three:
Bingo is a great game to start with because it is easy to learn and easy for children to understand. There are different types of bingo cards and it helps to know which are the best cards. I use a $10 bingo card with a picture of a bunny on it. The cards I used in my class were: "Wiggly," "Twisty," and "Crazy." When a player knocks the bunnies off the board, the players who have knocked the rabbits off get to keep the balls that they have drawn. If they draw a bunny with the "Big" or "Little" benny, they get the ball, if they knock out a "Bunny" with "Rabbit" written on the card, or if the bunny is drawn on a card that has a number, like, "1," they can keep that ball. This is great because players can win a lot of money at the same time. For the first few weeks, players will win $1, $2, and $3 at a time, depending on how much they play. During this time I'll give them a few bennies, so they won't get bored. Also, at first, it's best if players don't play the $5 card. It is the most expensive card and the least likely to come up. Once they are used to playing the cards, you can teach the more expensive cards like the ones with numbers, etc. At first I don' t allow the player to have more than one card in their hand, because I have noticed that the kids learn quickly and quickly forget. After a while, though, we can allow them more cards to use. Then we'll start playing for bigger prizes. We use $20 binnies and they win more money as they continue playing. When players are older, start them with only the larger binners. You can even have the game go by itself, where the person who wins the biggest prize gets to put the money in the bank. But I do recommend using the large binner cards in teaching

You can place limit orders by using the LOB order entry feature on the order book. You must be the first trader in line to be placed in the limit order. This means that you can’t place a limit in your own name.
Please note that each trader will have a different limit for each of his orders. Also, a trader can only place one limit at a time. If you have placed a large limit, you will be blocked from placing another limit of any size until you place your first limit with the same size as your last limit (for example, if you placed an $1,100 limit and then placed another $10 limit within the time frame of your other limit you would be unable to execute the $100 order until your limit size is reduced to $9).
This is true for both long and short limit positions. In a short position, the size you want to trade is determined by your existing position in that stock. So, by definition, there is no stock price. That means the market price of stock in Google is zero. But the book value of that stock, which is called the net asset value, is still the same. Hence, if the value is positive it means people are willing to buy more stock. If it's negative, people will sell more. And of course, that is why stock prices can be negative. Many people believe that bonds are for the purpose of financing purchases of securities that are considered safe and sound. I would not agree. Borrowing money for such purposes is simply not economically or legally viable. Bonds are issued to raise money to purchase securities and other assets that have a future value.
A bond is a promise to pay a certain amount of money in the future at a set date. The value of the bond at the set payment date is determined by the market and the underlying security. In other words, the value is dependent on the present worth of a company or other asset. If the company has no value, then the amount owed to the investor is zero. This is why the bonds have been called “an empty pledge.”
Bonds have no bearing on an asset’s value on a given date, but rather, are only an agreement to repay a fixed amount at that date in exchange for a premium. There is no guarantee that the payment will be made at all. A bondholder has the right to have the investment liquidated at any time before the scheduled payment. When it comes to bonds, you do not own the asset or the money, just the promise of payment in return for an investment. You do have an opportunity to sell the security in a secondary market, if you so desire, and you will receive the proceeds of any sale. However, there is nothing that can be done with the funds received from the sale of these securities other than to use them to repurchase the original issue of bonds from a new investor. That is, in essence, what a bond market is. It is not a place where you buy securities, or even an exchange where people buy and sell bonds. What you are buying is an interest rate on your money. Although the price of one bond may be higher than the next, it is still the same amount, paid in fixed payments. Likewise, when the prices of interest rates change, so will the cost of borrowing money and repurchasing bonds (and vice versa).

For example, the word balance is not typically used to mean the total due. Instead, a loan balance might be the sum of all loans you have outstanding. The word is more commonly used in the context of business loans. In that context, it is used as an accounting term to indicate that a certain number is owed on that loan. It is possible to make money by shorting a security. If the stock price is high, there is a good chance that it will go down, and a short position can be bought at a low price. But there are also times when the price goes down and there will be no profit.
The reason why this is not always possible is that the market will not give you any stock at or below the strike price you are short. The reason for this can also be that there may be an event that makes the security too expensive to buy or a company that is in financial difficulty that will make it too risky to hold. In other words, the profit-making period is only during the time that you have the right to purchase stock. As you can see, this type of short sale is an unprofitable one because you do not have any profit if the value of the underlying security is below its strike. A better way to enter the short side is to find a target that has a price that goes up, but a few months after you enter, you find that your target has become too cheap and you need to exit the position. This is the most profitable type and is called a swing trade. After entering the trade, make sure you stay long. That means that if your company offers a large group meal, and you eat most of it, it won't show up on the tax form. (Of course, if the meal is a big one, like a Christmas party, your boss may report to the IRS that it was a meal and therefore a taxable event, even if it wasn't.)

A bull puts spread is an option spread on a stock or other security.
It is also known as a put buy spread, or put option. A bull spread has the same characteristics as any other put or option trade, except that it is a bull trade and a profit is earned. The terms bull, bear, bullish and bearish have no special meaning. Bull spreads are popular in the stock market, where investors often look to purchase short-term puts in an effort to profit from the volatility of the market. With a bull put, the trader is trying to buy a call option and then sell the underlying stock in a single trade. If the option is exercised,
he or she will earn the premium received. Conversely, if the underlying stock is sold, he or her will lose the value of his or her original investment. This is the opposite of a spread trade where one contract is long one option against another option contract and one is short the other. In a traditional spread trade, one call is put and the next call, and so on. When a bullish spread is purchased, it means that the options are bought on the long side of each option by the short side of another call and put. For example, a trader who has a long call spread against a short put contract buys the call contract and sells the put contract to get a premium. Because the strike price is low, there is little profit in buying the bull call. However, because the price of options is volatile, buying a low strike puts (or selling a high strike call) is highly profitable because there will be a loss of value when they are exercised. Therefore, bulls put spreads have an inherent risk. Although the risk is small, investors are still encouraged to buy put options. Investors who do not want to take the chance of a big loss should not consider a purchase of this type of option trading. Another factor that influences the profitability of bulls put spreads is that there are no fees or commissions involved. There is no commission for the execution of buying or selling the contracts.

@David: I think you will be able to sell your shares for $1000 each at any time. However, there is a chance that the stock could trade down to $100 after the sale. There is no guarantee that your selling price will exceed the current market price. If you sell shares below your purchase price and the share price goes up, the difference is what you have to pay to buy the rest of the new shares. It will cost you more to replace them, so you should expect to lose money on the transaction. In other words, your total cost of selling your stake will probably exceed your gain. So, you may be better off buying more shares to increase your buying power. Of course, if you could buy them at an even higher premium than you paid, then you would be taking advantage of a situation in which you are more profitable than your competitors. In finance, the rate of returns on stock is the average rate at which a stock will return in a given time period. The rate is used in the calculation of the risk premium and the beta of a security.
The concept of rate can be generalized to incorporate the concept that the same stock might be worth different amounts at different rates of time. In this case, each rate represents a different time at the market. The difference in rates between a high-risk and a low- risk asset is called the alpha. This concept is often used as a measure of risk and return for portfolio management. For example, in an investment in common stocks, an investor might want to invest in companies with high alpha, but low beta. If the rates are different, then the return on the portfolio will be lower. Thus, risk is a function of both beta and alpha (the difference between the two rates).
A common method for calculating the stock market return is to use the Black–Scholes formula, which is based on a probability distribution function (pdf) for the price of an asset. However, this approach does not take into account the fact that stocks can have different market rates. One way to deal with this is by using the stochastic differential equation model to compute the expected return. Another way is using a stogeometric approach, where one can define the instantaneous rate (IR) of change of price. Stochastic processes are used to model the dynamics of prices, and to determine the IR. With the application of stogeyometric methods, one is able to consider the entire probability space of stocks and compute its IR and consequently, its expected rate. These two methods are discussed in depth in this paper.

Once you have that, the next important step is determining how long you think you can continue to make the contributions you want to. For example, if you are only making $10,500 per year, you might only have about $150,00 left to put away in the Roth. If you were to run out of funds, then you would have to dip into your savings, so the real question is what you're saving for. A Roth is not the best way to save for an emergency, nor is it the way for saving up for your future retirement income. 
If you've got a significant amount of unspent money in your Roth, or you simply don’t want the burden of making regular contributions to a traditional IRA (or other retirement plan), then the simplest way is just to keep it in cash. This is a great way of keeping your money without having to worry about tax liability or the possibility of losing your entire investment in retirement, which is why I personally recommend keeping it as cash in order to avoid having it tied up in something you cannot live without. Vested stock is a stock that has been issued with a security right to receive a certain amount of money (dividends) from the corporation on a yearly basis.
It is an investment vehicle that can be used to grow the value of the company. The value is increased by the amount that the stockholder is entitled to as dividends. This amount is usually calculated using the formula:
PV = P*V + D where PV is the price of stock, P is stock price, V is number of shares, and D is amount to be paid as dividend. If the number V and the dividend D are known, then the equation becomes: (P*(V+D))
This is similar to the simple interest equation used in a bank account. When a person deposits money to a checking account, the bank does not pay the person interest on the money deposited. However, if the same amount was deposited to an interest-bearing account and then withdrawn, at the end of each month the interest would be credited to that account until it was withdrawn. So, in the case of vested shares of a company, it is possible to have a negative balance in that company's account that would not be able to accrue interest. In other words, this means that in order to earn dividends, a share of equity in an unvested stock must be sold. And, to sell the equity, you must have some money. Dividend payments are usually in cash or other forms of payment, such as stock options or warrants. Thus, when a shareholder sells stock or equity to purchase a cash payment or a form of compensation, he or she will have to pay additional money, which is called the “diluted” dividend, into the share value, or the purchase price. To compensate for the dilution, equity owners must receive additional shares as compensation. As a result, shareholders must pay more money in dividends to make up for diluting the shareholder's equity. For example, if you are a farmer and you produce a product and that product is used to produce other goods, then the Fair taxing system is very similar to the system of taxation in which the government taxes the people on their production. That is, the farmers are taxed on how much of their goods they produce. A farmer who produces more goods than he uses is taxed at higher rates. If he produces less goods that he needs, he is given a refund. And if he doesn't produce anything, his money is refunded. All this is done at the same rate. So, there is no special treatment for any particular group. There is only a uniform tax rate applied to all. Because the rate is uniform, this will give every American a very fair tax payment. Dividends are payments that are made to shareholders. The most common form of dividend is a regular cash dividend. Other forms of dividends include share buybacks and stock repurchases.
You can think of stock dividends as a way for shareholders to share in the growth of a company, either through the issuance of shares and/or through share repurchase. Dividend payments are typically made when a stock's price is low and when the company is expected to make a profit. Stock dividends can be the result of an earnings announcement, or they can come from the companies own cash flow. It is important to understand that stock dividend payments do not have to be made at regular intervals. They can also come at any time during the year. For example, a large company that has recently announced an annual profit could decide to pay a dividend to its shareholders at the end of the fiscal year, rather than waiting until the following year to do so. This is known as the cash-flow dividend and the dividend would be paid to the shareholders in cash. As long as this company has the financial resources to meet its dividend obligation, it will continue to issue regular dividends to investors and pay them out in full every year as it has done in recent years. You should note that if a corporation has no intention of meeting its future dividend obligations, investors can become impatient and may take this as an indication that the corporation is failing to perform on its financial statements. The IRS has a complicated web of rules for calculating whether or not you qualify to claim a refund of taxes withheld. The IRS says it has to do so because the employer (you) didn’t pay the taxes, and because you didn't take the deductions the government required you to take.
When you file your 1040 with the IRS, you'll be asked to list all of the expenses you have deducted, the total you paid for them, how much you owe, etc. You can list whatever you want, but if you're not claiming a deduction, then you don't have to provide an itemization of what you deducted. For instance, if your total taxable income was $20,000 and you wrote off $1,500, your IRS Form 1098-C (statement of adjusted gross income) won't reflect that. (In that case, it probably wouldn't make sense for you not to include that $500 in your tax return.)
But when you claim your refund, there are still a few questions you must answer:

What is Commotities Commodity is a free market for commodities. In a commodity market, the only person who has the ability to buy or sell a certain commodity is the person that has it.
A commodity can be anything that can go from the ground up to the sky, from one person to another. Commutities can include anything from a bar of gold to a loaf of bread. The only way to determine the value of a given commodity, is by the price at which that commodity will trade. When a person buys a piece of wheat, for example, they are simply paying for the right to own that wheat and to use it to produce bread, and they will have to pay for this right at the time that the wheat is grown. This is called a "commodity".
In a commodities market people will buy and sell commodities based on the strength of the commodity and the demand for that particular commodity. If the people who produce the commodities do not have a demand, then they can not be sold, as they do nothing. Therefore the production of commodities has to be based upon the demands from those who desire them. With this in mind, one of my favourite quotes on commodity markets is from Charles Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities:
"It is not enough to say that one is buying the bread; one must say it is to eat or it will rot in the mouth. There must be a market."
This quote was given to me by a friend who told me that it was a quote from Adam Smith, who wrote The Wealth of Nations. It is clear that Smith did not believe that commodities can exist in a vacuum, that is, in an unregulated market. He believed that in order to exist, commodities had to have demand and supply. So, if the supply of something is low, people must buy it and if demand is high, there must not only be demand but there also must also be supply and it must work in tandem. For example, if you look at the number and size of daily trades for a given stock over a period of years, you get a picture that looks like the chart below. And I realized that the class I was taking was not really a course in economics, because it did not cover any topics or concepts that were not already taught in other classes. But it was a good introduction to the basics of economics.

In economics, optimal asset allocation refers to the allocation of a portfolio's assets in such a way that, at any given time, the portfolio is expected to have the highest expected utility or expected return. Optimization is a key concept in finance and economics.
There is no single optimal allocation. Some allocations are better than others. The question is to what extent and how much better. There are many different ways to answer this question, but the most common way is with the Sharpe ratio. This ratio is the ratio of the expected returns of two different portfolios. One of these portfolios is called the benchmark. It is an investor's starting portfolio and it is chosen at random. A second portfolio, called a reference portfolio or benchmark portfolio (or a benchmark) is constructed from a sample of stocks. In other words, it represents the average performance of all stocks over a long period of time. Its returns are then compared with those of other investors. If the returns from the second, benchmark, portfolio are higher than the return from some investor, then that investor is said to be better off than that other investor. An investor who is better-off than this benchmark is referred to as a superior investor and an inferior investor as an underperformer. So, if the investor can outperform the market by an amount greater than some factor, say 2%, then he or she is superior and the inferior as under-performers. Thus, a better performance by a factor of 2% or more is typically considered an exceptional performance. 
This type of analysis is sometimes referred as the economic justification for the term "superior".
The "best" portfolio can be any portfolio. For example, one might use a bond portfolio to earn the largest return on investment. However, even if one uses a single bond, there are numerous portfolios that can produce the same result. Likewise, an index portfolio might be the best portfolio for a given investor over the long term. Yet, investors might prefer to use index funds to reduce their risk. These differences are often referred in the literature as "opportunity costs". The opportunity cost of using a particular portfolio may depend on the time horizon (long-term or short- term), the investment horizon, and other factors. What matters is that the difference between the two portfolios with different characteristics can never be positive. That is, in order to make the comparison, we must take into account the opportunity costs that we would incur in using the other portfolio over some time period

Gross income means all income received from any source that is not subject to tax under the Arizona state income tax laws. Gross income includes compensation from wages, salaries, tips, commissions, bonuses, and other forms of remuneration that are not taxable as income.
Arizona income taxes are imposed on the first $5,000 of each individual's gross earnings from sources other than wages or salaries. The individual must file a return on or before the 15th day of the month following the end of any calendar quarter (Q3) in which the gross taxable income is received. In addition, if an individual has gross wages that total $1,500 or more during a calendar year, he or she must also file an income return for the year. Arizona income returns are filed on a monthly basis. Individuals who have gross incomes exceeding $100,00 in a single calendar month must submit a separate form for each calendar or fiscal year in excess of $300.00. There are no exceptions to the filing requirement. Any individual who files an Arizona return that contains an incorrect filing number or that does not include the taxpayer's correct federal filing status (i.e., single or married filing separately) will be subject, upon request, to an audit by the IRS. If the individual is audited and the return is found to be incorrect, the tax will either be abated or refunded. An individual may not change the amount of his or her gross annual income without the permission of IRS and must report any increase or decrease in his gross monthly income on Form 1040. For example, an increase in income from $2,100 to $3,200 would require a $400 increase on his Form. This increase could be either a decrease or an addition to his taxable gross in the following year (if his income for that year is $12,600). If he is single, his federal tax rate will only increase by $0.50. He may increase his state taxable amount by no more than $500. A married individual with gross total income of between $50,001 and $75,999 may only file if he has earned income over $10,150 in any one calendar (or fiscal) year and has also received wages over that amount. Married individuals with total gross tax of over 50,0001 may file on their own and not be required to file with their spouse. After an IRS audit, any tax refund will first be applied to reduce any additional tax owed

The word subsidy comes from the Latin word subsidium, which means "supplying."
Subsidies are commonly given in the form of a tax break. That is, the government gives a taxpayer some money in addition to the taxes they already pay. The government then uses the subsidy to help the taxpayer. A subsidy may be given directly or indirectly. Direct subsidies are given by the state or by a local or state agency. Indirect subsidies may come from employers, employers' employees or others. In all cases, there is usually a cost to giving the grant or subsidy. These costs are usually tax-deductible. Examples of indirect subsidies include corporate grants, sales tax breaks, and a variety of other things. Sometimes subsidies for one thing are called tax benefits, tax incentives, or tax preferences. All of these terms are used interchangeably.

The answer to the first question is simple: When a corporation is laying off employees, it's not necessarily the employees who are losing money. More often, the losses are the corporation's.
In the past, this has been a problem for the workers who were laid off. If their skills were not needed, they were terminated, and the remaining workers would have been less skilled and less motivated than before. The company would lose money, but the worker would be the one who would suffer. This is not the situation today. In today's economy, most corporations need only a few employees to be profitable. They don't need hundreds or thousands. And when they lay off workers, their losses tend to hit their stockholders in the form of lower dividends and lower stock value. But in most cases, when the workforce is reduced, companies don’t have to cut their prices to stay profitable, because they donâ€™t need as many employees. So they are able to raise their profits by reducing their labor costs. Of course, a reduction in labor cost is only possible if there are enough people who will do the work. A lay of the land in a big city or town can be a very profitable location for new business. However, even if a location is profitable for small businesses, there will always be many empty buildings and many vacant lots. This is the fourth in a series of articles on index investing. The first and second articles were published on March 27 and March 28, 2014, respectively.
The third article was published June 14, 2013. Today's article is about the tax implications of indexing. Index investing is a way to invest in the market without actually owning any individual stocks. This strategy involves buying and selling stocks without owning individual shares. You simply buy and sell index funds. These funds represent a composite index of the stocks in each market sector. When you buy an index fund, you are buying shares of an entire index and not any specific company. For example, if you want to buy shares in an S&P 500 index, a fund that tracks the 500 largest companies in America, then you would buy a basket of that index. In the same way, when you sell shares, the fund is selling a portion of its index portfolio. And when a portfolio is sold, it is not selling individual securities. So when someone buys an individual company's stock, that is buying a specific share of a stock in that company, and when they sell that stock they are not really selling the company as a whole. Instead, they may be selling one or two stocks of those companies, but they still own the companies as an entity. That is why a company can be sold in pieces, rather than being sold as one whole entity, which would be impossible to sell. A company might be broken up into many separate parts, each of which is separately traded on the stock exchange. One of these parts could be a manufacturing company that makes cars or trucks, or a shipping company which ships goods from one country to another. If a person wanted to trade in shares from the shipping business, he could sell those shares to someone who wanted shares that represented the transportation business. Or, perhaps he wanted the shares representing the manufacturing business and would sell them to a buyer who would purchase shares for the automotive business or the industrial business that manufactures cars. Each of this person's individual trades would represent the purchase and sale of shares within an overall index that represents the entire company and its entire industry. Since a corporation is made up of many different divisions, there are many stocks that are within each division, for example all of IBM's divisions are represented in IBM stock. But within those divisions there may or may not be individual companies that make up the divisions. There is no way that all the individual corporations making up IBM could all be represented within the index itself

Unemployment insurance is a system of temporary income support that provides benefits to workers who lose their jobs. It is funded through contributions from employers and employees and is intended to help workers during times of unemployment and the transition from unemployment to a job.
If you are unemployed, you can get unemployment benefits for up to 26 weeks. During this time you will be paid a sum of money called your benefit. The amount of your benefits is based on a number of factors, including your income and your job skills. If you were unemployed for more than 26 consecutive weeks, the state will deduct a percentage from your wages. This is called a “disability benefit” and it is paid as long as you qualify for it. After 26 straight weeks of being unemployed (the maximum benefit period) you may apply for a permanent job but that will take a lot longer to get. Once you have been unemployed long enough for the benefit to be deducted from wages, your unemployment benefit stops. You will not be eligible for any benefits until you find a new job or you get a state-approved job search. When you do find work, unemployment is over. (If your new employer is paying you less than the amount you would earn if you worked for them, they can take it out of future pay.)
There are different types of benefits you might qualify to receive. Many people are eligible to collect a benefit if they have lost their job due to no fault of their own. Others might receive a disability benefit, or a supplemental unemployment payment if their unemployment was due in part to an injury or illness. There are also a variety of different income-based benefits available to you that are intended for people who are either unemployed because they lost a regular job, due a reduction in hours, because the economy has changed, if a person is underemployed or unemployed due simply to circumstances beyond their control. Your eligibility for these benefits will depend on your age, length of time unemployed and other factors. Unemployment insurance covers a range of costs, from housing, transportation, food and medical expenses to lost wages and job training. These benefits can be a lifesaver. They can also be costly. Cash in the form of a dividend, or in any other form, does not incur tax on its receipt. However, the receipt of dividends is taxed when they are distributed.
(1) The distribution of an amount of cash from an investment account is taxable to the recipient, and the amount is subject to taxation in accordance with the rules of the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) with respect to income tax. The amount distributed is generally taxable in a taxable year in which the distribution is made. In addition, a distribution from a non-retirement account (a traditional or Roth IRA) is also taxable when it is distributed in that year. Distributions from other nonretiree accounts may be taxable only in later years. If the distributions are made before age 59½, they may also be subject in some circumstances to a 10% federal income-tax penalty. (2) A distribution in cash made to you is a ‘cash-in-lieu-of-dividend’ within the meaning of Section 736 of Subtitle C of Title 26 of US Code. You will receive a corresponding tax deduction equal to your share of any income taxes imposed on the dividend. A cash- in- lieu- of- dividend is not a deduction, however, because you will not receive any taxable income in return. Taxation for a cash in place is based on your tax rate at the time of distribution. For example, if you receive $1,000 in taxable dividends on $10,500 of nonqualified shares and pay no income or employment tax, you would receive no tax benefit. Because of this tax avoidance, it may have tax advantages. Therefore, before distributing a portion of your account to yourself, see if the account has any remaining taxable value. Most importantly, make sure that you are not receiving a tax-free dividend because of such tax benefits. I'm new to this site, and I'm curious as to why the Dow Jones Industrial Average is share price weighted.
It seems like a strange thing to do, since the index is based on the share prices of the companies in the S&P 500 index, which is a broader index. 
Is there some reason for doing this? And, if there is, what's its justification? I've read that the reason is that by weighting the stocks, it is harder for one company to influence the value of an index when its stock is not priced at its true value. Is that correct? If so, why is it better to weight the data by the stock price than by some other measure? What if the price of a stock changes but its earnings don't? Would the weight of that stock change? Is there any reason to use a measure other than the market price to determine the weights of all the constituent stocks in an equity index? Also, is the purpose to make the numbers of constituent companies smaller to reduce noise, or to increase the accuracy of index calculations? (And, assuming the former, can you think of any other reason?) Thanks. - Dave The weight is to ensure that a company's share in a market index doesn't influence its price too much. If that's what you're after, that can be accomplished by adjusting the weighted index's weightings. It doesn' really make sense to take the total weight from a single stock and divide it by its market value to get the percentage of ownership it has in that index (as if you were weight by shares). (The market weight, on its own, would be the same as the number of shares times the sum of each individual stock's market values.) The more you weight stocks by their market prices, the more they cancel each other out, resulting in less noise in your index calculation. (Although you can still get noise if your weighted market is too small or too large, so it's not ideal.)
There is no "reason" for weight. The purpose is simply to match up the relative performance of large and small companies. This is done by taking into account the past performance and future projections of both large companies and the small. These past and projected performance factors are multiplied by weights in order to balance out the large versus small differences in performance. In theory, this should be a more accurate representation of performance than an equal weighted portfolio

Synthetic options are a type of derivative product that are created from a single underlying asset. They have the advantage of being able to be traded on any exchange, and therefore their price can be easily calculated. The risk of these options is that they may be very volatile, with the price rising and falling over a short period of time.
To help with this risk, a derivative contract can have a limited time period to maturity. It can also be subject to a stop loss or a profit target. When trading options it is therefore important to consider the trade-off between the risk and the potential reward. This is what we will be looking at in this article. We will look at the different types of synthetic options, the risks they pose and how to calculate the expected return from each. Finally we’ll look into what you can do to reduce the chance of an option being a profitable trade. Let‘s get started.
What is a Synthetic Option?
A synthetic derivative is simply a product of the underlying stock and a certain number of options that will give it the same price as the stock. These options can either be binary options or fixed income options. In the case of binary, you will always be able predict the result of your trade, but if you are trading in the fixed-income market you have to make a decision to buy or sell at a particular price. A synthetic may therefore be any type from binary to fixed. For example, if the company you want to short the shares of is listed on the London Stock Exchange, then the synthetic would be a binary option. If you bought a call and you think that the share price is going to go up, your options would have been sold and your profit would show up on your trading account. However, when the value of shares goes down, it means that you“”were wrong and lost the premium, which is called a loss.
In the example above, we have two options: a C call option and an O put option, both of which are binary. Both options were sold in an attempt to predict where the prices of stocks and commodities would go. Once the profit or loss was calculated, these two products were created, using the original price of each share of stock as its basis. After the expiration of both the C and O, their value would then be calculated as if they were actual options on a stock, giving the investor a risk-free profit.

The term "day trading" has been used to describe a variety of strategies and practices. The terms are commonly used interchangeably, but they are not synonymous.
It is the practice of purchasing and selling securities at a specified time, and then buying and/or selling at another time. This trading strategy can be used by professionals as well as by amateurs. It is based on the concept that the price of the security will change in a predictable fashion, usually a few hours after the trading day has begun. Day traders usually buy before the market opens and sell after it closes. They may also use other techniques, such as buying at the opening, buying on a swing low, or buying in the last hour of trading, in order to capitalize on price changes that may occur at any time during the day. A day trader might trade a security in accordance with a "buy and hold" strategy, where the trader holds the securities until the value of them decreases to a level at which they can buy them. In some cases, day traders use futures contracts in place of stocks. Day trading is a form of speculation and trading in securities that do not have a proven business model. Some day trading strategies may be illegal depending on their nature. Traders who trade on margin may lose their money, as the margin requirements are higher for day-traders. However, many day trade funds and brokerage accounts offer no-risk accounts that allow daytrading. There are many different types of day trades. For example, some day brokers will allow their clients to daytrade stocks, options, futures, currency, commodity, etc. on an exchange. Others will only allow trading on securities, not commodities. The Bank was created by the British government to provide credit and financial services to commercial and industrial firms and to support the government's financial system. The bank's board of directors was made up of the governors of eight commercial banks.
The bank was granted a monopoly on the issue of paper money by Parliament, which allowed it to issue notes and coins in amounts not exceeding £20,000 per year. When a company sells an item, the new owner uses the old profits to purchase the item. If the items are in the form of money, then there must be a corresponding bank of accounts that contains the two sources of income: the cash and any other form such as stocks or property. (When selling a house, an up-dated bank statement shows the sale of the house and all associated expenses.)
In the case of a bookkeeper, he or she is responsible for keeping the books of account for a business or an individual, including the account to which the net income is deposited and one for which it is paid. It is important that the bookkeepers also keep a record of all of their financial transactions, even those involving a small amount of cash. In addition, there should be at least one bank and at most two to keep track of each of these accounts, and a separate ‘‘cash’‟ account, which represents any cash transactions made in their business. When a cash transaction is made, that money is either deposited into the ”up to date“ account or the bank. For example, if the person who sells a car makes a $100 cash deposit in his/her ’up until date account the $20 is taken out of that account and added to the sales account. Any other cash used in business is put into a cash account. This is different from a savings account which is used for short term savings. Thus, in a double entry book keeping system, all financial records are kept and no one is confused as to where the funds come or go. We're having a debate at work regarding whether banks are making more or less money when the interest rate is low. We think banks make less but are being told otherwise.
Our argument is that banks do not make money on the loans they make. They earn a fee and the fees are applied to the principal of the loan. The profit comes from the difference between the fee the bank charges and what the borrower pays. If the rate of interest on a loan is higher than the cost of funds on that loan, then the profit is greater. If it is lower, the banks net profit becomes negative. For example, suppose a bank makes a $100 loan at 12% interest. With the same loan the lender would have to pay $110 to get the $10 he loaned. His profit on this loan would be $9. That's a net loss of $1, or a loss for the year of -$1. This is true whether the economy is up or down. It does not matter whether interest is high or low as long as the money supply is fixed at $X and there is no inflation. So banks have a profit of zero when they lend money, even when there are higher interest loans available. Therefore, they are losing money. In fact, it's an open question as to whether or not banks lose money in the long run. (See here)
The issue we are having is whether to charge a higher rate when rates of return are lower. Many people believe that this is not the case. I would like to argue that it should be the other way around: banks should charge more when rate are high and lose more money if rates fall. This meant that people were actually paying about $25 for a piece of Facebook. Of course, this would only be true if you were holding Facebook on margin. Allocation is the process by which the State of New jersey allocates tax revenues to its political subdivisions in accordance with State law. The allocations are based on the assessed value of real property, which includes the land value (land value is equal to market value, adjusted for the fact that the tax base is generally comprised of unimproved land) and the value attributable to improvements, such as buildings, machinery, equipment, and personal property. All property assessed at over $500,000 is exempt from the transfer tax. Property assessed below $2,500 is subject to a transfer assessment. An allocation is made to each municipality for its share of taxes, based upon its assessed property value. This allocation process is accomplished by the County Tax Assessor, who calculates the taxable value for each taxable parcel of property in each county. Taxable value includes both land and improvements. If a municipality has more land than the county, the municipality is assessed a higher value than would otherwise be assigned to it if it were assessed only on its unimpeded land. Likewise, if a city has less land that a county it is assigned a lower value and vice versa. In this case, both the city and county are assessed the same value as if they had no land base. As a result of these adjustments, tax values on all taxable property are increased. For example, a taxpayer with a single-family residence and a parking lot with an assessed valuation of $50,001 receives an allocation of 50.0% of its tax bill to cover the cost of both its land ($5,007) plus the improvements ($12,008). David is the Founder and Chief Executive Officer of The Student Loan Center, a national non-profit organization that helps students get their hands on the student loan they need to make college possible. These costs can be significant, but many students don't realize they are not being fully compensated for them. Here are some common costs of going back to higher education and how you can find out if they're being properly compensated.
One of my favorite examples of opportunity cost is when you're in school and you've just been assigned a textbook for the first time. You can also contribute up $6,000 for the year. The tax treatment of an IRA depends on when you take it out of the plan. If you withdraw the money before age 59 1/2, you will have to pay tax on the withdrawal. But if you take it from age 60 1/(2) up until you retire, the tax will be deferred until you withdraw, then it will only be due when it is withdrawn. (See the IRS website: Also, if your wife and you have both contributed to the same IRA, your withdrawal can be tax-free. Then again, it depends which wife contributed. Only you can decide. Also remember that if the wife is your employer, she may be able to claim some of your retirement contributions for tax purposes. Your wife should check with her or her accountant. Finally, remember, IRA's are not like 401(k)s. They do not have a "lock-in" period. That is, once you start with an account, contributions will not roll over to another account at the same plan if they are taken out. As a result, there is no need to have another IRA when your first one is taken from the original plan because you'll be taking out more money the next year than you had in the first. This is particularly important if one of you changes jobs and loses your job. In that case, when the second IRA was taken it would be rolled over into the new job,
so you wouldn't have taken more out than the amount in your second plan when the first IRA plan was closed. For more information on IRA plans, see the "I RAs" link under "What is an Individual Retirement Account (I.R.A.)?"

I am not aware of any evidence for a negative relationship between the performance of a commodity future or stock, or other asset class, on the one hand, versus that of an asset, such as a Treasury bill or a stock market index, investment on another. In fact, there are a number of studies that demonstrate that commodities, as opposed to stocks or bonds, perform better when interest rates are low.
In the case of the Treasury bond market, the correlation is positive, but not significant. The Treasury market is a market where the returns are dominated by short term rates. If you go long Treasury bonds at very low interest rate, you will not make any money. Conversely, if you short Treasury securities at high interest, then you can make a lot of money with very little risk. For example, in July of 2014, when the yield on 10-year Treasury debt was 2.2%, a $1,000 investment in Treasury stock would have generated $2,816.00 (2.200% × $1000 = $21,800.40). In contrast, a similar investment could have earned $6,907.60 if invested in the same Treasury index fund. This is what I mean by the term “correlation is not causation.”
But in my opinion, one of three things could be happening here. It could mean that the bond markets are very good at predicting the future performance in a very short time period, which is in turn a reflection of their own efficiency. (This is the main argument for the use of futures contracts in many markets). It might also mean the market has a tendency to ‘stick’ to its own forecasts when investors are not looking. I have no evidence that supports my belief that bond prices ”stick to their guns“, although that does not preclude the possibility of other factors affecting bond returns. There are some studies which suggest that high bond yields are due to investor mispricing, since bond investors don‘t seem to be pricing in that they can invest in bonds and earn a higher return than cash. Finally, it could also be a case where bond traders are pricing their bets on market conditions being different from the current market environment. My belief is that these are all possibilities. The 10-year Treasury note is the most liquid U.S. government bond in the world. It is also the least-liquid, and is not traded in either the U- or C-class markets. That means there is virtually no liquidity for the market.
This means that the prices for 10yr bonds are set by the Treasury, not the central bank, which sets interest rates. So when the treasury sells 10 yr bonds, it sets the price. This means the yields on 10 yrs are higher than the yield on the 30yr. And the difference between the two yields is what the Fed pays for holding 10 year bonds (the yield differential) and the amount it pays to borrow 10 years (interest rate differential).
So when you look at the spread between 10 and 30 yer bonds in a given month, the monthly price is set not by market forces but by what is happening in treasury department, so the lower the interest rate the higher the bond price as the cost of borrowing the money is higher. The 10Y yield is lower than 30Y, but the premium on 30y is bigger than on 1Y. What is interesting to me is that when there was a financial crisis in 2007-08, you could not have told that from looking at interest spread. But now, that is exactly what you can see in spread in google finance or Yahoo finance. When the crisis hit, they saw a huge spike in spreads. From then on, when a crisis hits, all you see is a spike. Now, there are many reasons for this, including a higher inflation rate, lower interest as well as other things. but I think the main reason is because the fed pays less to hold bonds than to lend them. this is why when interest is high, bonds price goes up, as they are bought more to cover the high cost. Of course, if you think that bond prices are driven by interest and inflation, then you would think bonds would be at a premium right now. If you go back to the last time a big crisis happened, interest was low and bond spread was high. In fact, 30year and 10year bonds were at very low yield and spread for quite some time. Today, 10/30 and 1-10/1 are at high yield/spread, with 30 year at around 2.5% and a 1 year bond at only 1.2%.

I’m not talking about the United States, where the word is used in English but not in Spanish, or Switzerland, which uses ‘penny‘ in both languages. I am talking, of course, about Switzerland“s currency, the Swiss franc (CHF), which is not a cent.
Switzerland‟s Swiss Franc, known as the Franc, is the smallest currency in the world. It is a one-dollar-equivalent currency that is subdivided into 100 cents. The franc is pegged to the U.S. dollar at a rate of 1:1, and it is also pegged directly to other currencies. When you buy something in a shop, you will see the price of the item in Swiss currency. But when you take out your bank account statement, it will not show the amount you owe, but only the sum of money you have in your account. In other words, your money is kept separate from the bankÄôs money. Swiss banks are required to hold only Swiss banknotes, coins, gold, silver, platinum, palladium, diamonds, precious stones, gems, emeralds and rubies. They are not allowed to have any foreign currency (U.K. pounds, Japanese yen, Canadian dollars, etc.) in their vaults. You will find them in most Swiss shops, though, as long as itÖs not their duty to inform you. This is because the franc was used to create the value of Swiss debts during the Second World War, when it was the only currency left in circulation. Switzerland is, in fact, not very big, nor is it very rich. Its economy is based on the manufacturing of luxury goods and the export of these items. And its currency is only one of its assets. For example, if you want to buy an expensive car or watch, what you need is to find a dealer who can make a deal with a Swiss company that manufactures your desired item. So if Switzerland were to run out of dollars or francs, all the companies that use these currencies would go out-of-business. Their products would be worthless. After a stock is purchased by a company, the stock price gap closes. This is because the market believes that the company is likely to be acquired by someone else.
How do investors know this? They look at the valuation of the purchase price. If the price is too high, they think the acquisition is unlikely. But if the value is low, that means the buyer is highly likely. The higher the buy-out price, and the lower the target price of a competing company (the price the potential acquirer will pay), the more likely it is that a merger is in the works. So, if you are thinking of purchasing a position in a specific stock, you may want to do so before the gap between the current price and that of its most recent close is more than $1,500. A gap of this size indicates that there is a good chance the share price will move significantly higher (or lower) and then close it out within a few months. Because of stock splits and new share issues, a gap above $2,000 means that you can buy the shares at current market price (assuming it closes above the $3,600 mark) with a $200 gain. On the other hand, gaps below $500 mean you will have to pay $100 for the position. And, in between, there's a chance that it will take you a year or more to get your money back. There is no perfect formula for determining when a share is overpriced or underpriced, but the general rule is to wait at least a week after the close before buying. That way, after you've bought, it's clear whether the trade was a mistake or not. It's also important to understand the difference between a "gap" and a decline. During a short-term decline, an investor may see a brief gap in stock prices, which may indicate that something is going on in that company. A limit order is a type of derivative order that is used to limit the market price of a security (or other financial instrument) at a particular time. For example, if you have a call option for $100 and you are told that the price will be $120 at expiration, you can buy the option at $110 and sell it at the strike price $115. This is called a limit purchase (LPD) and is the opposite of an exercise. If you buy at 110, the stock will rise to $125 and if it falls to 110 the shares will drop to the exercise price. In this example you would sell at 115 and buy again at 120.
If you were to buy a put option with the same strike $135 and expiration date, it would be an LPD. The limit put order would allow you to sell the put at its strike at any time during the life of the contract. However, a sell order on the limit buy order has the effect of making the underlying share price go to zero at that time (the limit sell would not allow the buyer to make a profit if the security price falls below the buy limit).
With the rise in the use of limit orders, many market participants have begun to view limit buying and selling orders as a means of arbitrage between the different order types. A master limited partnership (“MLPs”) is an entity that was created to allow for the structure of a limited liability company (LLC) but to also allow the flexibility to provide a single shareholder with a return on investment. MLPs are commonly referred to as a “pass-through’ entity.
MLPS are generally structured as limited partnerships, which means that the investors‘ (the ‘partners) ownership of the MLP is limited to a percentage of stock ownership. In other words, only a portion of all the shares of MLPS is owned by investors. However, the shareholders in an MLSP can elect to have their ownership in the partnership be made up of both stock and other types of ownership (such as cash, real estate, etc.).
This option is known as the pass through option. The advantage of this option, over a traditional limited company structure, is that it allows for a larger return for shareholders, because the limited partners own a greater portion (or in some cases, all) of their investment in their MLPP. This is because in a MLSC, each shareholder owns a smaller proportion of shares, and therefore, they will not have the benefit of increased returns on their investments, by virtue of being able to participate in more of an investment than they would if they owned the entire stock of that company. Another advantage is the ability to avoid having the IRS treat the investor as an owner of any particular piece of property, or as having any liability for property. Under the pass through option the taxpayer owns the property outright, even if it is held by another person. Furthermore, if the company becomes a corporation, then the shareholder will be treated as being the owner. By contrast, a shareholder who is merely a stockholder in another LLC, would be considered an investor, not a proprietor, when the corporation is formed. Because the shareholding is only limited, there is no need to worry about the distribution of income. If the investment is in real property or in other property that is not considered part of your personal estate then you will have to include the costs of depreciation on your income tax return. Additionally, you can also avoid paying capital gains tax on the appreciation of real or other personal property you own, provided that you do not sell it. A put represents the right to sell the stock at some point in the future. We say "the right" because we usually have to give up something in order to get the option: We have the choice to buy the underlying stock, but we don't get to choose the price. However, the tradeoff is that we can sell our option at any time. If we want to profit from the difference between the market price and our strike price, we have a right but not an obligation to do so. The put price is the strike minus the dividend yield. That's why you have two strike prices: one for the regular stock and one that is offset by the risk-free dividend. As an example, if you buy a $1 stock for $10 and sell it for only $9, you've taken a loss. But if the company has a dividend of $0.50, that's the same as a profit of only 1 cent.
 You don' t have an option to pay the dividends. You can't buy back the shares you sold. And you don’t have any obligation whatsoever to keep the money if it ever goes away. (CNI)
A Canadian citizen or a non-resident for taxation purposes.
Citizens and residents of Canada are also known as "Canadians" or "residents" and for this purpose the term "non resident" is reserved. The term Canadian non Resident is used when the taxpayer does not live in Canada but is a resident in some other country or territory, for example, if the person is resident of the United States or United Kingdom. Some countries have a special rule for CNI that exempts them from paying taxes on income earned in the country and is called the Foreign Tax Credit (FTC).
The term is also used in reference to a person who is not a Canadian resident but has a permanent residence in a country. This person would be a "Canadian nonresident" for Canadian tax law purposes but would not be eligible for the FTC. 
For the purpose of Canadian income taxes, a CNC is any person whose principal place of residence is outside Canada and whose permanent address outside of Ottawa is at least 100 kilometres from the capital. A CNR is anyone who has no permanent Canadian address. The box numbers (39-38) on a tax return are the boxes to be used for the tax calculations.
Box 39 is the box for tax payable on income and box 37 is for net tax. The first number in the middle is how much tax is due and the second number is what the total amount of tax due is. If the numbers are added together, it equals the net amount owed. This is used to calculate the amount that is reported on line 22 of the return. It does not mean the entire amount due, only the part due to tax on total income. For example, if I have $100,000 in net income, that means the $10,010 tax owed is not all of my total net taxable income of $110,100. That part of net $101,900 is taxable to me, and is in box 3. Box 3 is taxable, but not taxable. So, the taxable portion of income is $9,990, which is shown on Line 2 of Form 1040. In addition, I owe $200,500 in taxes, so I also owe line 5 on Form 1120. I am only taxed on my income that I actually owe, not on all that might be taxable, such as interest income on bank accounts. Because the IRS has made changes to the way taxes are calculated on some income types, we should always double check our tax returns to make sure that we have the correct amount reported correctly. This is a discussion on Collecting dividends while insulationing volatility with options within the The Second Best forums, part of the General Discussions category; I'm still waiting for my dividends to come in, but I think I got a decent idea how I can collect them, and it's not a bad one.
I think that you can ...
If you're bullish on the stock, you buy a call option. The strike price is the current stock price, $40, so the premium is $4. If you own the call, the price will rise to $41. Your option is worth $1 because the strike is at $45. You receive the dividend, which is equal to the option price. (The total dividend is actually $3.50, because you have to pay $2 for the options and $.75 for dividends).
You then buy the put option, paying $5 for it. As the value of your stock falls, your put will become more valuable. When the market rises, it will drop to zero, giving you a profit on your call. And you will collect a dividend. This is an easy way to collect dividends, without having to sell stock. It is also a way of insuring your dividend by buying options that will fall in value if the company is doing poorly. Since you are guaranteed a $10 dividend if your company tanks, this is like having a safety net. However, there are some caveats. First, if you use this technique to buy options for all of a company's stock for a long time, eventually the dividends will stop. Second, when you sell the stocks, they will be worth less than the premiums you paid for them. Third, since the companies are doing better than you think, their dividends may increase in a few months. Also, many companies have a lot of debt and are not going to be able to make good on their liabilities. Therefore, using this method will not guarantee you any dividends. But it may be a good hedge against a stock market crash. I hope this helps. - J

When a company tells investors that it’s going to be acquired by another company, that acquisition is announced, and the acquisition price is given as a number. That number can be anywhere from $0 to $100 million. It is very rare for the number to change, but when it does, it typically does so by a small amount.
That is not the case with the latest acquisition of Best Buy. On Monday, BestBuy.com announced the purchase of the troubled electronics retailer Bestbuy.org for $3.3 billion. This was not a $2 billion buyout, as was reported, this was a massive buyback. Best buy.co reported the following:
Best Buy is acquiring Bestbuys.Org for about $10.7 billion, including debt. The price represents a 20% premium to the best-buy site‘s closing price on Friday. However, the actual number that Best Buys will pay for BestBuys is $17.1 billion for a premium of 32%. So, when Best BUY announced that they were going buy BestBUYS, they did not say that the price was going up to a certain level, or that their stock was getting more expensive, etc. In other words, what they actually said was, we are going ahead with this deal and we expect to pay a lot more for it. So this is a very important distinction. What they are saying is, “we are buying Best buys”. They are not buying it for more money, nor are they paying more. They are also required to record all the transactions that are made with their customers' funds. While the bank may not be required (as a matter of course) to make a record of every transaction with its customers, it would be unwise for it to do so. There are many reasons for this, but one of them is the possibility that there may be a mix-up between the records kept by the customers and the record kept in the banking system. For example, a customer may deposit money into a savings account, which then is transferred to a checking account. The depositor may forget to write down the source of the money (e.g., savings or checking), and this is a possibility. This could also happen if the customer does not always pay the same amount in each of his or her accounts. In such cases, there is always a chance that, by mistake, an account has not been transferred in accordance with what the depositors have told the account holder. As a result, when the accounts are reconciled, they may show that no money has ever been deposited. At the very least, this would cause the fund to be deemed "unavailable."
If a person purchases property, and then later withdraws the property from a different account than the one originally used to purchase it, then there would have to have actually been a withdrawal from the original account before the purchase could have taken place. State plans have two characteristics that make them different from defined-contribution plans:
The benefits are more complex than if you were to invest in an individual retirement account (IRA) that allows for tax-free growth. The benefit package typically consists of benefits based on a participant’s salary and years of service. State plans do not have this benefit. If the participant retires before the age of 60, the benefits in the state system are zero. For example, if a plan participant retired at age 55 and the benefit amount was $1,000 a month, then at the end of the month the full amount would be withdrawn. But if the same person worked for 10 years and then retired, he would receive a benefit of only $900 per month. In the case of a state retirement system, all the person would get is that $100 per paycheck, although the employee may also be eligible for any unused balance of his or her account. It is also possible to combine the two types of plans. An individual‘s account in a retirement plan could be classified as a “state plan” if it is defined by the laws of its state. There are two important advantages to a definition by state law: First, a person“s retirement benefits may be less complex, and second, state plans are better protected from inflation.

Why do investors hold the investment bankers' hands and not their own? Because the banks have access to the same information as the investors. They have all the data available on how the business is being run, how it makes money, what its competitors are doing, whether it has any 'weak links' and so on. I think the question is not "why options" but rather "Why do options exist?"
(As a side note: options are also used in the context of "commodities", but I don't think that is what you mean.)
The answer lies in "option pricing".
Suppose you have a stock you own that pays a dividend. (Of course you don’t.) The stock pays dividends in regular intervals, and the dividend is currently worth x. But the stock also has options that grant the holder the right to buy the underlying stock for an amount greater than x, at a price between $y and $z.
For example, suppose the price of the options is $x-y$ and that the value of x is 10. Suppose also that you want to exercise the option at the current price, but the market is in fact at $10$. You can exercise it by buying the full amount of stock at 10, paying the $5 dividend, selling the shares, then buying back the same number of shares at 11 and paying $1. You will have made a profit of $4. So, you should exercise your options at that price. It‘s the difference between the initial price and what the strike price is that makes the profit. This is the idea of option pricing. In your example the cost of buying stock is x and you are paid a $3 dividend in addition. The cost to you is therefore x-3. That is, the number you pay for the share is 3x. If the company wants to increase the dividends, it can raise the x price to x+3, making your profit $2. Since the increase is worth 3, this is called a "call option". If it wants a decrease in dividends to y-1, a call option would be worth -3x to the owner of that option. A put option is a similar thing, except that it has a strike of z-x, where z is some fixed number.

C = S*(1 + r)

However, there is a growing literature on the idea of using the standard deviations of returns instead, a standard measure that is more intuitive. This paper seeks to understand how the true volatility (the standardised volatility) compares to the volatility that would be estimated using historical returns. We consider a number of different approaches to measuring the return volatility and assess the performance of these measures in terms of their accuracy in predicting the future volatility. The paper also compares the approaches using a sample of US stocks, and shows that the risk-adjusted measure outperforms the other measures.
Historical volatility is one of the most commonly used measures of risk in financial markets. One way to measure the “true volatility” of an asset is to use the difference between the actual historical price and its forecasted price. While this approach is intuitive, it does not take into account the randomness in the forecast. For example, suppose that a forecast is generated by using an algorithm that, on average, has a 70% probability of generating a price that lies within a 20% range of its actual price at the end of a year. In this case, the price will be 70/200 times higher than its expected price, which is 20%. This measure is not a good measure for the expected risk of future price changes. Therefore, we propose a measure to estimate the real volatility, by taking into consideration the probability distribution of price returns, instead of only considering the mean of return. More specifically, our measure uses the conditional variance of past returns conditional on a particular time period, where we take the variance conditional upon the realised price in that time-period as the measure.
